linerNotes.title: Amateur Night at the Apollo
linerNotes.body:
Amateur Night at the Apollo began in 1934, and it has been called the toughest crowd in show business ever since. The audience is the judge: cheer and you stay, boo and you are escorted off. On November 21, 1934, a teenager named Ella Fitzgerald signed up to dance, changed her mind at the last minute, sang instead, and won. Sarah Vaughan won in 1942. The Jackson 5 won in 1967.

Before they go on, contestants rub the Tree of Hope for luck. It is a piece of an elm that stood outside the Lafayette Theatre on Seventh Avenue, a few blocks away, where performers used to gather. When the city widened the avenue in 1934 the tree was cut down, and a piece of it found its way to the Apollo stage. I have checked: it is a stump, and it has more fans than most people.

linerNotes.title: 1520 Sedgwick Avenue
linerNotes.body:
On August 11, 1973, Cindy Campbell threw a back-to-school party in the recreation room of 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the West Bronx, to raise money for new school clothes. Her big brother Clive, known as DJ Kool Herc, played the records. Most histories mark that night as the birthday of hip hop.

Herc was born in Kingston, Jamaica, and came to the Bronx in 1967. Jamaica's sound systems, with their huge speakers and a DJ who was the star of the night, shaped how he threw a party. His big discovery was that dancers went wildest during the break, the short stretch where the band drops out and the drums carry on. So he played two copies of the same record and switched between them, stretching a few seconds of break into minutes. He called it the Merry-Go-Round. Every DJ who has ever looped a beat owes that move a thank-you.

linerNotes.title: The Chitlin' Circuit
linerNotes.kicker: Harlem to the South Side - 1920s to 1960s
linerNotes.body:
Under segregation, Black performers built careers on a road map of their own. In the 1920s the Theatre Owners Booking Association, or TOBA, booked Black acts into theaters across the South and beyond; performers tired of low pay and hard terms joked that the initials stood for Tough On Black Artists. After TOBA collapsed in the early 1930s, a looser network of theaters, clubs and juke joints took its place. It became known as the Chitlin' Circuit, after the soul food dish.

Its crown jewels were the big city theaters: the Apollo in Harlem, the Howard in Washington, the Royal in Baltimore, the Regal in Chicago and the Uptown in Philadelphia. If you could win over those rooms, you could win over anywhere. The circuit faded after the civil rights victories of the 1960s opened other doors, but its stages trained generations of the greatest performers in American music.

linerNotes.title: Messages in the Dead Wax
linerNotes.body:
Look past the last song on a record and you reach the run-out groove, the smooth band of vinyl around the label that collectors call the dead wax. Etched or stamped there is the matrix number, the code that matches each side to its master. Extra letters and numbers can show which cut of the lacquer a copy came from, which plant pressed it and, often, the initials of the mastering engineer.

Some engineers left more than initials. In Britain, George Peckham was known for scratching 'A Porky Prime Cut' and little jokes into the wax, and plenty of others hid messages there for anyone curious enough to look. Collectors use these marks to identify first pressings, because the dead wax often holds details the printed label leaves out. Philly note: the Uptown Theater on North Broad Street, opened in 1929, was the city's great soul showcase, where DJ Georgie Woods produced shows from the late 1950s.

linerNotes.title: The Howard and Black Broadway
linerNotes.body:
The Howard Theatre opened on August 22, 1910, at 620 T Street NW, billed as the largest colored theater in the world. That was more than twenty years before the Apollo became Harlem's showcase. The Howard anchored a stretch of U Street so full of theaters, clubs and Black-owned businesses that it was nicknamed Washington's Black Broadway.

Duke Ellington grew up in the city and was known for winning band contests at the Howard. Over the decades its stage launched or welcomed Ella Fitzgerald, the Supremes and Washington's own Marvin Gaye, along with countless revues. The theater was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1974, closed in 1980, and reopened on April 9, 2012 after a restoration of about $25 million. Thirty-two years dark, and then the lights came back on.

linerNotes.title: Go-Go: The Beat That Never Stops
linerNotes.body:
Go-go is Washington's own music, and it is built for a live band. In the 1970s guitarist and singer Chuck Brown and his band, the Soul Searchers, became the name most tied to a way of keeping a dance floor moving without a single gap: songs flow into one another, held together by congas, cowbells and a steady, swinging drum pocket. The band calls out to the crowd and the crowd answers, a call and response with deep roots in the Black church.

Brown's late-1970s hit 'Bustin' Loose' carried the sound far beyond the city, and he became known as the Godfather of Go-Go. Bands like Rare Essence, Trouble Funk and Junkyard Band kept it growing, many of their players trained in D.C. school marching bands. Chuck Brown died in 2012. In February 2020 the District of Columbia made go-go its official music.

linerNotes.title: The Funk Brothers
linerNotes.body:
Motown's hits had famous faces on the sleeves, but a great many of them were played by the same house band, the Funk Brothers. From 1959 to 1972 they worked in Studio A, a converted garage at 2648 West Grand Boulevard that the musicians called the Snakepit. Their ranks included keyboardists Earl Van Dyke, Joe Hunter and Johnny Griffith, drummers Benny Benjamin, Uriel Jones and Richard 'Pistol' Allen, guitarists Robert White, Eddie Willis and Joe Messina, percussionists Jack Ashford and Eddie 'Bongo' Brown, and bassist James Jamerson.

For years their names did not appear on the records. Apart from a few releases under Earl Van Dyke's own name, the first Motown album to credit them was Marvin Gaye's What's Going On in 1971. Wider recognition came decades later: the 2002 documentary Standing in the Shadows of Motown, two Grammys in 2003, and a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2004. Several of them did not live to see it.

linerNotes.title: James Jamerson and the Unnamed Bass
linerNotes.body:
James Jamerson was born in 1936 on Edisto Island, South Carolina, moved to Detroit as a teenager, and became the bass player on a huge share of Motown's hits of the 1960s and early 1970s. He started on upright bass, moved to a Fender Precision, and played with a single finger of his right hand, a technique he called the Hook. His lines ran, syncopated and sang, and changed what bass players everywhere thought the instrument could do.

Like most session players of his era, he was rarely named on the records. Recognition came mostly after his death in 1983. Allan Slutsky's 1989 book about him, Standing in the Shadows of Motown, later gave the documentary its name, and in 2000 the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inducted him as a sideman, alongside drummers Earl Palmer and Hal Blaine. On old soul records, the bass player is often the missing name.

linerNotes.title: The Warehouse and the Regal
linerNotes.body:
House music took its name from a club. From 1977 to 1982 the Warehouse, at 206 South Jefferson Street, was home to DJ Frankie Knuckles, a New Yorker who had arrived in Chicago at 22. He blended disco, soul, gospel-strong vocals and electronic records, re-edited them and later added drum machines, for a mostly Black, largely gay crowd that danced until morning. Regulars called the club the House, and by most accounts the music took that name. Knuckles won the first Grammy for Remixer of the Year, and in 2004 Chicago named a stretch of Jefferson Street after him. He died in 2014.

A few miles south stood the Regal Theater, opened in 1928 on South Parkway, now King Drive, near 47th Street in Bronzeville. The giants of jazz and R&B played it, and B.B. King recorded Live at the Regal there in 1964. It was demolished in 1973.

linerNotes.title: First Avenue and the Name Fight
linerNotes.body:
First Avenue began as a Greyhound bus depot built in 1937. It opened as a music club called the Depot on April 3, 1970, and after a couple of name changes it has been First Avenue since the early 1980s. Its outside walls are covered in painted stars, each carrying the name of an act that played there. One star is gold: Prince's. He first played the club in 1981 and filmed the concert scenes of Purple Rain there.

Prince also fought one of the most famous ownership battles in music. In a dispute with Warner Bros. over control of his work, he announced on his 35th birthday, June 7, 1993, that he would be known by an unpronounceable symbol, and he appeared in public with the word 'slave' written on his cheek. In April 2014 he reached a new agreement with Warner that gave him ownership of the master recordings he had made for the label.

linerNotes.title: Sister Rosetta and Beale Street
linerNotes.kicker: Memphis, Tennessee and the sanctified church
linerNotes.body:
Before rock and roll had a name, Sister Rosetta Tharpe was playing it in church clothes. Born in Cotton Plant, Arkansas, in 1915, she grew up singing and playing guitar in the Church of God in Christ, where her mother was an evangelist. From her first Decca records in 1938 she carried gospel into theaters and nightclubs, and by the 1940s she was playing electric guitar with a bite and swing that later rock and roll stars studied. The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inducted her as an early influence in 2018.

Beale Street in Memphis was where Black Southern music came to town. W.C. Handy published 'The Memphis Blues' in 1912 and 'Beale Street Blues' in 1916. In the late 1940s a young guitarist working as a radio DJ was billed as the Beale Street Blues Boy, soon shortened to B.B. King. In 1977 Congress declared Beale Street the Home of the Blues.

linerNotes.title: From Congo Square to the Second Line
linerNotes.body:
In the late 1700s and early 1800s, enslaved and free people of African descent gathered on Sunday afternoons at an open field on the edge of New Orleans, now called Congo Square, to drum, sing and dance. It was one of the rare places in the slaveholding South where African rhythm was kept alive so openly.

It runs through the second line. Social aid and pleasure clubs parade on Sundays behind a brass band; the club and band are the first line, and everyone dancing along behind them is the second. That parade beat shaped the city's studio drummers. Earl Palmer, who drove early hits for Fats Domino and Little Richard, said you could always pick out a New Orleans drummer by the parade beat in his bass drum. From there came the funk of the Meters, and brass bands like the Dirty Dozen (1977) and Rebirth (1983), who brought funk and hip hop back to the street.

linerNotes.title: DJ Screw and the Slab
linerNotes.body:
In the early 1990s a Houston DJ named Robert Earl Davis Jr., known as DJ Screw, began slowing records way down and chopping them, repeating and stuttering phrases by playing two copies against each other. The result, chopped and screwed, is heavy and spacious, so every word lands. He made his mixtapes at home, and the local rappers who freestyled on them became the Screwed Up Click. His gray cassettes, more than 350 of them, sold from his house and later from his own shop, Screwed Up Records and Tapes. He died in 2000, at 29.

The music fits the car culture it rode in. A slab, a name commonly said to stand for slow, loud and bangin', is a classic car with candy paint, wire wheels that poke out from the body, called swangas, and a trunk that opens to show off neon lettering. Slow music, slow cruise, everybody looking.

linerNotes.title: Atlanta Builds a Sound
linerNotes.body:
Atlanta's story starts with bass. MC Shy-D's 1988 track 'Shake It', produced by a young DJ Toomp, is often credited with bringing Bronx-style hip hop to the city, and booming, 808-heavy Southern bass kept the clubs and car stereos full. In 1989 L.A. Reid and Babyface founded LaFace Records in Atlanta, later home to TLC and Toni Braxton, and Jermaine Dupri's So So Def followed in 1993.

Then came the basement. The production team Organized Noize built layered soul and funk tracks for OutKast and Goodie Mob in Rico Wade's basement, the Dungeon, and the Dungeon Family helped put the Dirty South on the map. Lil Jon drove crunk, all party chants and big drums, from the late 1990s into the 2000s. In the 2000s producers including Shawty Redd, DJ Toomp and Zaytoven helped shape trap: rolling hi-hats, dark keys and 808s that hit like weather. That sound has since spread across popular music worldwide.

linerNotes.title: Miami Bass and the 808
linerNotes.body:
Roland released the TR-808 drum machine in 1980, and at first few people wanted it. Then producers in Miami found out what its kick drum could do when tuned low and left to ring: a bass note you feel in your chest. By the mid-1980s that boom, fast tempos and call-and-response party chants added up to Miami bass. MC A.D.E.'s 'Bass Rock Express' is often cited as the first hit of the style, producers like Pretty Tony and local labels spread it across the South, and 2 Live Crew, with Luther Campbell's own label, carried it nationwide.

Miami bass grew up in a city of Black American, Caribbean and Latin neighborhoods, with a shared love of big outdoor sound. Its records also travelled south: DJs in Rio de Janeiro took Miami bass and built funk carioca on it. And that same 808 kick later anchored Atlanta trap. One machine, a whole family tree.

linerNotes.title: Out of the Trunk
linerNotes.kicker: Oakland and the Bay Area - 1960s to now
linerNotes.body:
The Bay Area learned early that you do not need a major label to find an audience. In 1983 Oakland's Too $hort released his first album on a local label, 75 Girls Records and Tapes, and sold tapes by hand. His 1987 album Born to Mack is estimated to have sold about 50,000 copies, largely from the trunk of his car, before Jive Records reissued it. In Vallejo, E-40 sold tapes store to store on consignment and built his own label, Sick Wid It Records, in the early 1990s.

The groove came first, though. The Bay gave the world Sly and the Family Stone in San Francisco and Tower of Power in Oakland, both formed in the late 1960s. Decades later came hyphy: the word was first said on record by East Oakland's Keak da Sneak in the mid-1990s, and Mac Dre and others turned it into a whole party culture of its own.

linerNotes.title: G-Funk and the Talkbox
linerNotes.body:
G-funk took the funk of the 1970s and slowed it down for the car. Dr. Dre's 1992 album The Chronic set the template: deep bass, laid-back tempos, high whining synth lines, and samples and replays of George Clinton's Parliament-Funkadelic. The sound ruled West Coast rap through the mid-1990s.

Its other voice was the talkbox, a tube that carries an instrument's sound into the player's mouth so it can be shaped into words. Roger Troutman of Dayton, Ohio, made it his signature with his band Zapp in the early 1980s, Zapp's grooves were sampled all over West Coast rap, and Roger played talkbox on 2Pac's 'California Love' in 1995. He died in 1999. As for the cars, lowrider culture grew from Mexican American car clubs in Los Angeles in the 1940s and 1950s; by around 1959 hydraulics let a car rise and drop at the flip of a switch, and clubs across South L.A. made the culture their own.

linerNotes.title: Arena Pop and the Video Color Line
linerNotes.body:
MTV launched on August 1, 1981, and in its first years it played very few videos by Black artists, presenting itself as a rock channel. That began to change in 1983. Michael Jackson's 'Billie Jean' video premiered on MTV in March 1983, and it is generally credited as the first video by a Black artist to go into heavy rotation. Accounts differ on how hard his record company had to push. A few Black artists had been on the channel before; this card says heavy rotation on purpose.

Music television helped make the 1980s the decade of the arena R&B and pop star, with shows of choreography, costumes and production as ambitious as the records. Arenas like the Forum in Inglewood, opened in 1967, became the standard stage for that era. Black audiences already had a channel of their own: Robert L. Johnson had launched BET in 1980.

linerNotes.title: The Moulin Rouge
linerNotes.body:
In the 1950s Black stars headlined the big showrooms of Las Vegas but could not stay, gamble or eat in many of the hotels whose stages they filled. Sammy Davis Jr., headlining at the Frontier, had to lodge in a rooming house on the city's Westside, the Black neighborhood across the railroad tracks, as did other Black performers of the time.

On May 24, 1955, the Moulin Rouge opened on the edge of the Westside as the first racially integrated hotel-casino in the United States, integrated from the staff to the guests to the stage. By many accounts, stars came over after their own Strip shows to catch its late show. It closed that October, after barely five months. But in March 1960 city and business leaders met with the NAACP and agreed to end segregation on the Strip and downtown. The deal is remembered as the Moulin Rouge Agreement.

linerNotes.title: Black Britain on the Dance Floor
linerNotes.kicker: London and the North of England - 1970s to now
linerNotes.body:
In the summer of 1988 Wembley Stadium hosted seven sold-out shows on Michael Jackson's Bad tour, about 504,000 people in all, a Guinness record at the time. Britain's love of Black American music ran deep long before that: in the 1970s, Northern Soul all-nighters at clubs like Wigan Casino (1973 to 1981) packed dance floors with rare American soul records.

Black Britain also made sounds of its own. Lovers rock, sweet romantic reggae from South London, had one of its biggest hits in Janet Kay's 'Silly Games', written and produced by Dennis Bovell, a UK number 2 in 1979. Pirate radio stations, often broadcasting from tower-block rooftops, carried the new music; Kiss FM began as a pirate in 1985. In the early 1990s jungle sped breakbeats up to 160 to 170 BPM. In the early 2000s grime came out of East London at about 140 BPM, and Dizzee Rascal's Boy in da Corner won the Mercury Prize in 2003.

linerNotes.title: Japanese Pressings and Listening Bars
linerNotes.body:
The Tokyo Dome opened on March 17, 1988, and that December Michael Jackson played nine sold-out shows there on his Bad tour. Japan's devotion to Black American music also lives in much smaller rooms. Japan's music cafes, where people come to listen closely, go back to the 1920s, and the jazz kissa, or jazz listening cafe, became an institution. Soul and funk bars followed, often run by owners whose record collections are the whole point of the visit.

Japanese pressings of American soul and jazz are collector favorites. Many came with an obi, a paper strip wrapped around the edge of the sleeve with the title in Japanese, and an insert of liner notes written in Japanese, often with the lyrics transcribed and translated. A missing or torn obi can cut a record's value sharply. Fun fact: collectors argue about whether the pressings really sound better, but nobody argues about the care that went into them.

linerNotes.title: Bucharest, October 1, 1992
linerNotes.body:
On October 1, 1992, Michael Jackson played Bucharest's National Stadium, now the Lia Manoliu Stadium, on the last night of the first leg of his Dangerous World Tour. The stadium was sold out. HBO broadcast the concert, the special set a ratings record for the channel at the time, and it was released on DVD in 2005 as Live in Bucharest: The Dangerous Tour.

The date mattered. Less than three years earlier, Romania had overthrown the Ceausescu regime, under which Western records were hard to get. Music came in suitcases from abroad, over Radio Free Europe and Radio Luxembourg, and above all on cassettes copied from friend to friend, again and again. Listening to Western radio could draw the attention of the secret police. So a whole generation knew this music from tapes dubbed so many times the hiss was part of the song, and then saw it played live in their own city.

linerNotes.title: The Montreux Jazz Festival
linerNotes.body:
Claude Nobs, who worked for Montreux's tourist office and loved jazz, founded the Montreux Jazz Festival in 1967 with Geo Voumard and Rene Langel. The first edition ran three days and featured Charles Lloyd's quartet with Keith Jarrett and Jack DeJohnette. When the Montreux Casino, the festival's home, burned down during a concert on December 4, 1971, the fire inspired Deep Purple's 'Smoke on the Water', and Nobs became the 'Funky Claude' of its lyrics.

The festival recorded nearly everything, and some of the great live documents of Black American music were made by the lake: Les McCann and Eddie Harris's Swiss Movement in 1969, and Nina Simone's intense 1976 concert, one of the most famous performances of her career. Quincy Jones later co-produced the festival, and in 1991 Miles Davis played Gil Evans's arrangements there with Quincy conducting. Nobs died in 2013.

linerNotes.title: Jazz Americans in Europe
linerNotes.body:
For many Black American musicians, Europe offered work, audiences who listened closely and a break from segregation at home. Josephine Baker arrived in Paris in 1925 and became one of the biggest stars in France. Sidney Bechet, the New Orleans clarinet and soprano saxophone pioneer, settled in France in 1950 and was a huge star there until his death in 1959. Drummer Kenny Clarke, one of the architects of bebop drumming, made Paris his home from 1956, and pianist Bud Powell lived there from 1959 to 1964.

Tenor saxophonist Dexter Gordon moved to Europe in 1962 and based himself in Copenhagen for about fourteen years. In 1986 he played an American jazz musician living in Paris in the film 'Round Midnight' and was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actor. They carried the music with them, and a generation of European players learned it at their elbows.

linerNotes.title: Kwaito to Amapiano
linerNotes.kicker: Johannesburg and Gauteng, South Africa - 1990s to now
linerNotes.body:
Kwaito grew up alongside South Africa's democracy. In the early 1990s, as apartheid ended and Nelson Mandela took office in 1994, young producers in Soweto and other Johannesburg townships slowed house music down and layered on local melodies, percussion and chanted vocals in township slang. Its name is usually traced to the Afrikaans word kwaai, meaning angry or cool. Arthur Mafokate, Boom Shaka, M'Du Masilela, TKZee and Mandoza were among its stars.

About twenty years later came amapiano, a name meaning the pianos. It emerged in the townships of Gauteng in the mid-2010s, and people still argue over exactly where. It blends deep house, jazzy keys and kwaito's unhurried swing, and its signature is the log drum, a deep, percussive, sliding bassline; percussive basslines like it go back to kwaito producers such as M'Du. This is South African house music and its own family, separate from West African Afrobeats.

linerNotes.title: Essence Fest and the Sound of the 90s
linerNotes.body:
In 1995 Essence magazine marked its 25th anniversary with a three-day party in New Orleans over the Fourth of July weekend, with Luther Vandross and Gladys Knight among the stars. It was meant to happen once. Instead the Essence Festival became an annual gathering, concerts in the Superdome by night and talks, food and community by day. After Hurricane Katrina it moved to Houston for 2006, then came home in 2007. People come back year after year, and many treat it as a kind of family reunion.

Its early years ran on the sounds of the time. New jack swing, named by writer Barry Michael Cooper in 1987 and shaped by producer Teddy Riley, put R&B singing over hip hop beats. Then neo-soul, a label credited to executive Kedar Massenburg, brought back live instruments and classic soul warmth, with albums like D'Angelo's Brown Sugar (1995) and Erykah Badu's Baduizm (1997).

linerNotes.title: From Spirituals to Swing
linerNotes.body:
On December 23, 1938, producer John Hammond put the family tree of Black American music on the stage of Carnegie Hall in a concert called From Spirituals to Swing. Sponsored by the left-wing magazine New Masses and dedicated to Bessie Smith, who had died the year before, it moved through spirituals and gospel, blues, boogie-woogie and big-band swing in a single night.

The bill included Mitchell's Christian Singers, Sister Rosetta Tharpe, harmonica player Sonny Terry, Big Bill Broonzy, singer Big Joe Turner with pianist Pete Johnson, boogie-woogie pianists Albert Ammons and Meade Lux Lewis, and the Count Basie Orchestra. Hammond had hoped to present Robert Johnson, but Johnson had died that August, and Broonzy was recruited in his place. A second concert followed on December 24, 1939. The recordings from both nights are still one of the best maps of where R&B and rock and roll came from.

linerNotes.title: Marian Anderson at the Lincoln Memorial
linerNotes.body:
In 1939 the contralto Marian Anderson, already acclaimed in Europe and America, was refused the use of Constitution Hall in Washington, run by the Daughters of the American Revolution, because she was Black. First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt resigned from the organization in protest, and Interior Secretary Harold Ickes helped arrange for Anderson to sing outdoors instead.

On Easter Sunday, April 9, 1939, she sang on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, opening with 'My Country, 'Tis of Thee', before a crowd of about 75,000, with millions more listening on the radio. In 1955 she became the first African American soloist to sing at the Metropolitan Opera. And in 1978, when the Kennedy Center in Washington presented the first Kennedy Center Honors, Marian Anderson was among the first five people honored. Thirty-nine years after a Washington hall shut its doors to her, the nation's arts center put her name at the top of its list.

linerNotes.title: Amen, Brother and the Funky Drummer
linerNotes.kicker: The breaks that built hip hop - 1969 and 1970
linerNotes.body:
Hip hop was built on breaks, and every break was played by a real drummer. In 1969 the Winstons, a soul group from Washington, D.C., released 'Color Him Father' with a B-side called 'Amen, Brother'. In the middle is a drum break of about seven seconds played by Gregory C. Coleman. Sampled and resliced, the Amen break became the backbone of jungle and drum and bass and has turned up in thousands of tracks. Neither Coleman nor bandleader Richard L. Spencer, who held the copyright, received royalties for those samples. Coleman died in 2006. In 2015 a fan-run fundraiser sent Spencer about 24,000 pounds as a thank-you.

In March 1970 James Brown released 'Funky Drummer', with a loose, improvised break by Clyde Stubblefield. It has been sampled on more than a thousand records. Stubblefield had no songwriting credit on the track, so he received no royalties from those samples. He died in Madison, Wisconsin, in 2017.

linerNotes.title: Just Out of the Spotlight
linerNotes.kicker: Behind the lead singer - 1960s to now
linerNotes.body:
Some of the most famous voices in pop belong to singers whose names many listeners never learned. Darlene Love sang lead on 'He's a Rebel', a number one hit in November 1962 released under the name of the Crystals, who did not sing on it. With her group the Blossoms she sang behind many of the biggest acts of the 1960s, and in 2011 she was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

The Sweet Inspirations, with Cissy Houston, sang behind Aretha Franklin on her Atlantic records in the late 1960s and backed Elvis Presley in Las Vegas in 1969. Merry Clayton's voice cracks open the Rolling Stones' 'Gimme Shelter' (1969). Their stories reached a wide audience in the documentary 20 Feet from Stardom, which won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature in 2014. Next time a chorus lifts you off the ground, look up who was singing just out of the light.

linerNotes.title: Watch Night: Freedom's Eve
linerNotes.body:
On the night of December 31, 1862, enslaved and free African Americans gathered in churches and homes, many in secret, and waited for midnight. On January 1, 1863, President Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation would take effect, declaring free the enslaved people in the states then in rebellion. People prayed, sang and kept watch until the new year arrived. That night is remembered as Freedom's Eve.

Watch night services were older than that night: Moravian churches held them in the 1700s, and John Wesley brought them into Methodism around 1740. But December 31, 1862 gave the service a new meaning in Black churches, and the tradition has continued on New Year's Eve ever since. In many congregations people still pray through the last minutes of the year, and some still call out the old question from Isaiah: 'Watchman, what of the night?' Freedom was not finished on January 1, 1863. People kept watching anyway.

linerNotes.title: How to Read the Credits
linerNotes.body:
Every recorded song has two lives: the composition, meaning the melody and words, and the master, one particular recording of it. Songwriters and their publishers own shares of the composition and are paid when it is performed, sold or streamed; organizations such as ASCAP (founded 1914) and BMI (1939) collect performance royalties for them. The master usually belongs to whoever paid for the recording, often a label, unless the artist owns it.

On a credit list, look for written by (the songwriters), produced by (whoever shaped the recording), the performers and session players, the engineers, and sample credits, which name the recordings and songs a track borrows from. Using a sample usually takes permission for both the recording and the composition. Streaming services such as Spotify added fuller songwriter and producer credits in 2018. Minneapolis note: Prince's 1978 debut, For You, famously read 'Produced, arranged, composed and performed by Prince.' Read the small print. - T.
